title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: A great drug company does not sell pills; it sells decades of restored organ function.
epigraph.author: Clinical Biopharma Operating Principle

web_blocks.html: Vertex runs as a single reporting unit focused on drugs for serious specialty and rare diseases [1, 2]. Beneath that accounting structure, the business in late 2026 rests on five commercial and late-stage pillars [2, 5, 6]. They are: (1) Cystic Fibrosis (CF), (2) Hematology and Gene Editing (Casgevy), (3) Pain (Journavx), (4) Rare Endocrine Diseases (Crinetics/Palsonify, closed September 1, 2026), and (5) Renal/Nephrology (povetacicept PDUFA November 30, 2026; inaxaplin Phase 3) [2, 5, 6].

In FY2025, Vertex posted $12,001.3 million in total revenue, up 9% from $11,020.1 million in FY2024 [1, 2]. That sum included $11,970.6 million in net product sales and $30.7 million in other revenue [1, 2]. Cystic Fibrosis brought in roughly $11.80 billion, or over 98% of total revenue [2]. Trikafta/Kaftrio alone drove $10,312.7 million (85.9% of total revenue), while new Alyftrek added $837.8 million (7.0%) [2]. Legacy CF drugs (Kalydeco, Orkambi, Symdeko/Symkevi) plus other products made up $820.1 million, including Casgevy ($115.8 million) and Journavx ($59.6 million) [2]. By Q3 2026, quarterly revenue hit $3.44 billion (+12% YoY) [5]. U.S. sales reached $2.17 billion (+10% YoY), and International sales hit $1.27 billion (+16% YoY) [5].

web_blocks.takeaway: CF still represents ~96% of Q3 2026 revenue ($3.30B of $3.44B), though Alyftrek ($706M in Q3 2026) is rapidly cannibalizing/upgrading Trikafta while Casgevy ($99M) and Journavx ($58M) scale sequentially [2, 3, 4, 5]. *Derived/residual from disclosed totals.

web_blocks.html: Each pillar solves a concrete medical problem. In Cystic Fibrosis, a patient with two F508del mutations makes a misfolded CFTR chloride channel [13]. Because that protein never reaches the cell surface, thick mucus clogs the airways and pancreas [13]. Trikafta and once-daily Alyftrek pair two 'correctors' that guide the protein to the cell wall with a 'potentiator' (ivacaftor or deutivacaftor) that props it open [8, 9]. For a 12-year-old CF patient starting therapy today, lung function (ppFEV1) jumps 10–14 percentage points within weeks [8, 13]. Flare-ups drop sharply, and projected survival has moved from the thirties toward near-normal life spans [8, 13].

Casgevy uses a very different clinical and supply-chain model [10]. A young adult with severe sickle cell disease and painful crises visits a hospital Authorized Treatment Center (ATC) [10]. Doctors collect their stem cells and ship them to a specialized plant [10]. There, CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing turns fetal hemoglobin (HbF) back on by disabling the BCL11A enhancer, and the cells are frozen [10]. Next, the patient undergoes inpatient busulfan chemo to clear their bone marrow before a one-time infusion [10]. This turns a lifelong disease into a functional cure. Vertex logged >500 treatment starts by Q1 2026 and $99 million in Q3 2026 sales [3, 5, 10].

Journavx (suzetrigine) serves a wholly different setting: acute pain after surgery [11]. A patient leaving the hospital after knee or abdominal surgery needs strong pain relief without opioid euphoria, breathing risk, or addiction [11]. Journavx blocks NaV1.8 sodium channels found only on peripheral pain nerves, not in the brain [11]. It stops pain signals before they reach the central nervous system [11]. By Q3 2026, Journavx hit $58 million in quarterly sales [5]. It passed 1 million cumulative scripts in Q1 2026 and filled ~535,000 scripts in Q2 2026 [3, 4].

Vertex's newest pillars expand its specialty reach into endocrinology and kidney care. Through the September 2026 Crinetics deal, Palsonify (paltusotine) gives acromegaly patients a daily pill instead of painful monthly injections [5, 6]. It added $10 million in its first partial month in September 2026 (~$24 million total Q3) [5, 6]. In kidney care, povetacicept (from Alpine Immune Sciences, PDUFA November 30, 2026) blocks BAFF and APRIL cytokines to cut toxic IgA in IgA nephropathy [5, 7, 12]. Meanwhile, oral inaxaplin (Phase 3 AMPLITUDE, interim readout early 2027) blocks toxic APOL1 pores in APOL1 kidney disease [5, 12]. Outside the U.S. and Europe, Vertex out-licensed povetacicept in 2025 to Zai Lab (Greater China and Singapore) and Ono Pharmaceutical (Japan and South Korea) rather than building a standalone Asian renal salesforce [1].

web_blocks.title: Why Alyftrek Cannibalization Is Margin-Accretive
paragraphs: At first glance, Alyftrek's fast climb to $706M in Q3 2026 ($573.6M in Q2 2026) looks like self-cannibalization of Trikafta [4, 5].

In fact, moving patients from twice-daily Trikafta to once-daily Alyftrek extends core CF patents from 2037 to 2039 [9, 13]. It also cuts Vertex's royalty rate from ~10% down to the low single digits, lifting net profit per patient [9, 13].

web_blocks.html: Beyond its five lead pillars, Vertex runs a high-risk clinical pipeline for diseases that lack good cures [12]. In Type 1 diabetes (T1D), zimislecel (VX-880) is a stem-cell islet therapy that restores natural insulin in severe cases [12]. It still requires chronic immune suppression after Vertex recorded a full $379.0 million intangible asset impairment charge in Q1 2025 to write off its encapsulated VX-264 T1D program acquired from Semma Therapeutics [1]. In muscle disease, VX-670 targets myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) with a small molecule [12]. Together with Crinetics' atumelnant (Phase 3 congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Phase 2 Cushing's syndrome) [6], the pipeline spans four drug modalities. Using small molecules, biologics, CRISPR editing, and cell therapy guards against single-tech obsolescence.

book_paragraphs: On paper, Vertex Pharmaceuticals reports its business as a single operating segment. If you only glanced at the segment footnote in the Form 10-K, you might assume it is still a one-product company. Yet if you walk through the clinic doors where Vertex's medicines are actually prescribed in late 2026, you will find five distinct businesses operating under one roof—each with its own biology, customer journey, and economic rhythm.

The undisputed anchor remains Cystic Fibrosis, which still accounts for roughly ninety-six percent of Vertex's $3.44 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue. To appreciate why this franchise behaves like an annuity, picture a child born with the F508del mutation. Without treatment, a defective chloride channel causes thick mucus to trap bacteria in the lungs and block digestive enzymes in the pancreas. Trikafta—and now its once-daily successor, Alyftrek—fixes that channel at the molecular level. Patients take pills every single day for life, and because stopping therapy causes lung function to deteriorate again, adherence and persistence are extraordinarily high.

What is fascinating about Alyftrek's surge to $706 million in quarterly sales by Q3 2026 is that Vertex is deliberately migrating its own Trikafta patients onto the newer pill. Why cannibalize your own $10 billion blockbuster? Two reasons: Alyftrek simplifies dosing to once a day with slightly better sweat-chloride reductions, and it pushes core CF patent exclusivity out to 2039 while cutting external royalty payments from roughly ten percent down to the low single digits.

Outside cystic fibrosis, the other four pillars look radically different. Consider Casgevy, the CRISPR gene-edited therapy for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia. This is not a pill you pick up at CVS. It is a months-long hospital choreography: harvesting a patient's stem cells, shipping them to a cleanroom for CRISPR editing, wiping out the patient's bone marrow with chemotherapy, and infusing the edited cells back in. Revenue reached $99 million in Q3 2026—impressive sequential growth, yet still a fraction of a single quarter of Trikafta.

When you step back and look at all four commercial and late-stage pillars together, a clear strategic pattern emerges. Vertex refuses to compete in crowded, commoditized primary-care arenas where ten interchangeable molecules fight over formulary rebates. Even in acute pain with Journavx — its broadest commercial market — Vertex targeted a non-opioid mechanism where hospital systems and surgeons have a powerful clinical and regulatory incentive to reduce post-operative opioid prescribing.

In rare endocrinology, the September 2026 Crinetics acquisition follows that exact same playbook: Palsonify replaces burdensome monthly injectable somatostatin analogs with a once-daily oral pill for acromegaly, while atumelnant targets congenital adrenal hyperplasia with a first-in-class oral mechanism. Every segment Vertex enters is anchored by high unmet need, clear clinical differentiation, and concentrated specialist prescribers.

book_callouts.title: Following the Patient Journey, Not Just the Molecule
book_callouts.text: Notice the contrast between Trikafta and Casgevy. Both are scientific triumphs, yet one scales via a specialty pharmacy refill every thirty days, while the other scales one hospital bed and conditioning regimen at a time. Never assume a breakthrough therapy's revenue curve will look like a small-molecule pill.

book_subsections.title: Pain, Endocrinology, and the Renal Frontier
paragraphs: Vertex's third pillar, Journavx, tackles a massive, crowded market: acute pain. By blocking NaV1.8 sodium channels strictly in peripheral nerves, Journavx relieves post-surgical pain without touching the brain's opioid receptors. By Q3 2026, it was generating $58 million per quarter on the back of hundreds of thousands of prescriptions—proving real commercial demand, even though payer prior-authorization friction and a setback in chronic sciatica have tempered early blockbuster euphoria.

The fourth and fifth pillars are where Vertex has deployed its checkbook. Through the September 2026 acquisition of Crinetics Pharmaceuticals, Vertex added Palsonify—a once-daily oral pill for acromegaly that replaces painful monthly injections—alongside late-stage candidate atumelnant for congenital adrenal hyperplasia. And in renal medicine, povetacicept awaits a November 30, 2026 FDA decision in IgA nephropathy, backed by Phase 3 inaxaplin for APOL1-mediated kidney disease. Together, these five pillars represent Vertex's bid to ensure that when 2037 arrives, cystic fibrosis is no longer its sole engine of survival.

book_subsections.title: Geography, Patient Persistence & the Real-World Pipeline
paragraphs: Geographically, Vertex's revenue split in Q3 2026—$2.17 billion in the United States and $1.27 billion internationally—shows that its franchise is genuinely global. International revenue actually grew sixteen percent year-over-year in the third quarter, outpacing the ten percent growth in the U.S. as newly negotiated reimbursement agreements in Europe and other developed markets brought younger pediatric cohorts and Alyftrek onto national formularies. Because national health systems in Europe negotiate multi-year portfolio agreements, international CF revenue tends to be remarkably sticky once access is secured.

Behind those five commercial pillars sits a second wave of clinical bets that could reshape the company in the 2030s. Zimislecel is Vertex's stem-cell-derived islet therapy for Type 1 diabetes, aiming to restore natural insulin production—an extraordinary scientific goal, though still gated by the need for immunosuppressive drugs especially after Vertex took a $379.0 million full impairment charge on its encapsulated VX-264 T1D program in the first quarter of 2025. VX-670 targets myotonic dystrophy type 1, a severe inherited neuromuscular disorder with no approved disease-modifying therapy. When you step back and look at the whole map, Vertex is no longer a one-trick CF company in scientific scope—even if CF still pays ninety-six percent of the bills today.

Pipeline durability also requires honest accounting for clinical setbacks and patent cliffs. In Q1 2025, Vertex recorded a full $379.0 million intangible asset impairment charge to write off VX-264, the encapsulated type 1 diabetes program acquired from Semma Therapeutics. That write-off left zimislecel as the sole clinical islet-cell candidate, and zimislecel still requires chronic immune suppression.

At the same time, the legacy cystic fibrosis portfolio faces its first wave of generic exposure in 2027. Both Kalydeco and Symdeko lose U.S. patent exclusivity in 2027, shifting commercial reliance onto Trikafta through 2037 and once-daily Alyftrek through 2039. Converting eligible patients onto Alyftrek before 2027 protects both market share and patent runway.

book_subsections.title: Why Every Vertex Therapy Targets a High-Friction Specialist Channel
paragraphs: Walk through a real-world prescribing scenario in each pillar and you immediately see Vertex's commercial moat. For a cystic fibrosis patient carrying at least one F508del mutation, a pediatric pulmonologist at an accredited CF center writes a single electronic prescription that routes through a specialty pharmacy hub, securing prior authorization and lifetime daily adherence. In sickle cell disease, a hematologist refers a transfusion-dependent patient to an Authorized Treatment Center where stem cells are harvested, CRISPR-edited in a cleanroom, and re-infused after busulfan conditioning — a complex, one-time curative journey priced above $2 million.

Meanwhile, in acute pain, an orthopedic surgeon discharges a knee-replacement patient with a 14-day oral course of Journavx, avoiding opioid addiction risks while navigating hospital pharmacy and PBM tiering. Each therapy sits in a distinct clinical workflow, yet all share high physician urgency and clear clinical value.
